items.sentence_de: Ich liebe dich sehr.
items.sentence_translation: I love you very much.
items.grammar_tip: 'Dich' is the accusative (direct object) form of 'du'. Use it when 'you' are the one receiving the action.

items.sentence_de: Er kommt aus Berlin.
items.sentence_translation: He comes from Berlin.
items.grammar_tip: 'Er' is the masculine singular pronoun used for men or masculine nouns (der).

items.sentence_de: Es ist heute sehr kalt.
items.sentence_translation: It is very cold today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Es' is the neuter pronoun used for neuter nouns (das) or impersonal expressions like the weather.

items.sentence_de: Ich heiße Thomas.
items.sentence_translation: My name is Thomas.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ich' is always the subject of the sentence and the verb usually ends in -e.

items.sentence_de: Das Haus ist nicht groß.
items.sentence_translation: The house is not big.
items.grammar_tip: Use 'nicht' to negate adjectives, adverbs, or verbs. Use 'kein' only for nouns with indefinite articles.

items.sentence_de: Wie heißen Sie?
items.sentence_translation: What is your name?
items.grammar_tip: 'Sie' is the polite form for 'you' and is always capitalized, whether singular or plural.

items.sentence_de: Wann beginnt der Film?
items.sentence_translation: When does the movie start?
items.grammar_tip: 'Wann' is used for questions about time or dates.

items.sentence_de: Warum lernst du Deutsch?
items.sentence_translation: Why are you learning German?
items.grammar_tip: 'Warum' asks for a reason. The verb always follows immediately in second position.

items.sentence_de: Was ist das?
items.sentence_translation: What is that?
items.grammar_tip: 'Was' is used to ask about objects, things, or actions.

items.sentence_de: Wer ist der Mann?
items.sentence_translation: Who is the man?
items.grammar_tip: 'Wer' is used to ask about the identity of a person (the subject).

items.sentence_de: Wie geht es dir?
items.sentence_translation: How are you?
items.grammar_tip: 'Wie' is used for manner, names (Wie heißen Sie?), or state of being.

items.sentence_de: Wir wohnen in München.
items.sentence_translation: We live in Munich.
items.grammar_tip: 'Wir' is the first person plural pronoun. The verb ending for 'wir' is always -en.

items.sentence_de: Wo ist mein Schlüssel?
items.sentence_translation: Where is my key?
items.grammar_tip: 'Wo' asks for a static location. Do not confuse it with 'wohin' (direction).

items.sentence_de: Woher kommen Sie?
items.sentence_translation: Where do you come from?
items.grammar_tip: 'Woher' is used to ask about origin, usually paired with the verb 'kommen'.

items.sentence_de: Wohin gehen wir heute?
items.sentence_translation: Where are we going today?
items.grammar_tip: 'Wohin' indicates movement toward a destination or direction.

items.sentence_de: Es ist acht Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: It is eight o'clock.
items.grammar_tip: Numbers in German are not capitalized unless they are used as nouns.

items.sentence_de: Das Auto ist neu.
items.sentence_translation: The car is new.
items.grammar_tip: 'Das' is the definite article for neuter nouns in both the nominative and accusative cases.

items.sentence_de: Ich trinke den Saft.
items.sentence_translation: I am drinking the juice.
items.grammar_tip: In the accusative case (direct object), only the masculine article 'der' changes to 'den'.

items.sentence_de: Der Tisch ist alt.
items.sentence_translation: The table is old.
items.grammar_tip: 'Der' is the nominative article for masculine nouns. It changes to 'den' in the accusative.

items.sentence_de: Die Frau ist Lehrerin.
items.sentence_translation: The woman is a teacher.
items.grammar_tip: 'Die' is used for all feminine singular nouns and all plural nouns regardless of gender.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe drei Kinder.
items.sentence_translation: I have three children.
items.grammar_tip: German numbers are straightforward; 'drei' is used just like 'three' in English.

items.sentence_de: Woher kommst du?
items.sentence_translation: Where do you come from?
items.grammar_tip: Use 'du' for friends, family, and children. The verb ending for 'du' is usually -st.

items.sentence_de: Du bist sehr nett.
items.sentence_translation: You are very nice.
items.grammar_tip: 'Sein' (to be) is irregular. 'Du bist' is the second person singular informal form.

items.sentence_de: Du hast einen Hund.
items.sentence_translation: You have a dog.
items.grammar_tip: The verb 'haben' is slightly irregular for 'du': the 'b' is dropped (hast instead of habst).

items.sentence_de: Du sprichst gut Deutsch.
items.sentence_translation: You speak German well.
items.grammar_tip: 'Sprechen' is a stem-changing verb where the 'e' changes to 'i' in the 'du' and 'er/sie/es' forms.

items.sentence_de: Das ist ein Tisch.
items.sentence_translation: That is a table.
items.grammar_tip: In the nominative case, 'ein' is used for both masculine and neuter nouns.

items.sentence_de: Das ist eine Lampe.
items.sentence_translation: That is a lamp.
items.grammar_tip: Feminine nouns use 'eine' for both nominative (subject) and accusative (object).

items.sentence_de: Ich kaufe einen Apfel.
items.sentence_translation: I am buying an apple.
items.grammar_tip: Masculine nouns change from 'ein' to 'einen' when they are the direct object of a sentence.

items.sentence_de: Das kostet eins Euro.
items.sentence_translation: That costs one euro.
items.grammar_tip: 'Eins' is the cardinal number, but it drops the 's' when followed by a noun or 'Uhr'.

items.sentence_de: Meine Schwester ist elf Jahre alt.
items.sentence_translation: My sister is eleven years old.
items.grammar_tip: 'Elf' is a basic number and does not change its ending.

items.sentence_de: Er fährt mit dem Bus.
items.sentence_translation: He is going by bus.
items.grammar_tip: The verb 'fahren' changes its stem vowel from 'a' to 'ä' in the 2nd and 3rd person singular.

items.sentence_de: Er hat einen Bruder.
items.sentence_translation: He has a brother.
items.grammar_tip: The verb 'haben' is irregular; notice it loses the 'b' in the 3rd person singular 'hat'.

items.sentence_de: Sie ist meine Freundin.
items.sentence_translation: She is my friend.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ist' is the 3rd person singular form of the highly irregular verb 'sein'.

items.sentence_de: Ich besuche euch morgen.
items.sentence_translation: I will visit you all tomorrow.
items.grammar_tip: 'Euch' is the accusative form of 'ihr' (you plural), used when 'you all' is the object.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe fünf Euro.
items.sentence_translation: I have five euros.
items.grammar_tip: Numbers like 'fünf' are used as adjectives and do not require endings before nouns.

items.sentence_de: Es ist jetzt halb acht.
items.sentence_translation: It is half past seven now.
items.grammar_tip: In German, 'halb' refers to the hour to come, so 'halb acht' means 7:30.

items.sentence_de: Das Ticket kostet hundert Euro.
items.sentence_translation: The ticket costs one hundred euros.
items.grammar_tip: 'Hundert' is used for 100; you can also say 'einhundert' for more emphasis.

items.sentence_de: Ich bin Studentin.
items.sentence_translation: I am a student.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bin' is the 1st person singular of 'sein'. Remember: no article is needed for professions in German.

items.sentence_de: Ich darf hier parken.
items.sentence_translation: I am allowed to park here.
items.grammar_tip: Modal verbs like 'dürfen' have no ending in the 1st person singular.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe zwei Katzen.
items.sentence_translation: I have two cats.
items.grammar_tip: 'Habe' is the standard 1st person singular form of 'haben'.

items.sentence_de: Ich heiße Markus.
items.sentence_translation: My name is Markus.
items.grammar_tip: Verbs ending in '-ßen' like 'heißen' only add '-t' instead of '-st' for the 'du' form.

items.sentence_de: Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.
items.sentence_translation: I can speak German.
items.grammar_tip: The modal verb 'können' changes its vowel from 'ö' to 'a' in the singular forms.

items.sentence_de: Ich kaufe heute ein.
items.sentence_translation: I am going shopping today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Einkaufen' is a separable verb; the prefix 'ein-' always moves to the very end of the sentence.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte einen Tee.
items.sentence_translation: I would like a tea.
items.grammar_tip: 'Möchte' is a polite way to express a wish and follows modal verb rules (no ending for ich/er/sie/es).

items.sentence_de: Ich muss jetzt gehen.
items.sentence_translation: I must go now.
items.grammar_tip: The modal verb 'müssen' changes its vowel from 'ü' to 'u' in the singular.

items.sentence_de: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.
items.sentence_translation: I get up at six o'clock.
items.grammar_tip: 'Aufstehen' is a separable verb; 'auf-' moves to the end of the main clause.

items.sentence_de: Ich will Pizza essen.
items.sentence_translation: I want to eat pizza.
items.grammar_tip: 'Wollen' is a modal verb; notice the vowel change from 'o' to 'i' in the singular.

items.sentence_de: Ich kenne ihn gut.
items.sentence_translation: I know him well.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ihn' is the accusative (direct object) form of 'er'.

items.sentence_de: Woher kommt ihr?
items.sentence_translation: Where do you all come from?
items.grammar_tip: Use 'ihr' when talking to a group of friends or children.

items.sentence_de: Ihr habt ein schönes Haus.
items.sentence_translation: You all have a beautiful house.
items.grammar_tip: The plural 'ihr' form of 'haben' is regular: stem + 't'.

items.sentence_de: Hallo Kinder, ihr seid heute sehr fleißig.
items.sentence_translation: Hello children, you are very hardworking today.
items.grammar_tip: Use 'ihr seid' for the second person plural.

items.sentence_de: Das ist leider kein Tisch für uns.
items.sentence_translation: Unfortunately, that is not a table for us.
items.grammar_tip: 'Kein' negates masculine and neuter nouns in nominative.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe heute leider keine Zeit mehr.
items.sentence_translation: Unfortunately, I have no more time today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Keine' is used for feminine or plural nouns.

items.sentence_de: Wir brauchen heute keinen Saft aus dem Laden.
items.sentence_translation: We don't need any juice from the store.
items.grammar_tip: 'Keinen' is the accusative form for masculine nouns.

items.sentence_de: Besuchst du mich morgen in der Stadt?
items.sentence_translation: Are you visiting me in the city tomorrow?
items.grammar_tip: 'Mich' is the accusative form of the pronoun 'ich'.

items.sentence_de: Meine Tochter ist jetzt schon neun Jahre alt.
items.sentence_translation: My daughter is already nine years old now.
items.grammar_tip: 'Neun' follows 'acht' in the counting sequence.

items.sentence_de: Die Vorwahl für diese Stadt beginnt mit null.
items.sentence_translation: The area code for this city starts with zero.
items.grammar_tip: 'Null' is the number zero in German.

items.sentence_de: Wir treffen uns morgen Abend um sechs Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: We are meeting tomorrow evening at six o'clock.
items.grammar_tip: 'Sechs' is the number after five.

items.sentence_de: Meine Eltern kommen aus Berlin, sie wohnen dort.
items.sentence_translation: My parents come from Berlin, they live there.
items.grammar_tip: 'sie' is used for the third person plural.

items.sentence_de: Das ist Maria und sie lernt gerade Deutsch.
items.sentence_translation: This is Maria and she is learning German.
items.grammar_tip: 'sie' (lowercase) is the feminine singular pronoun.

items.sentence_de: Jeden Abend im Bett sie liest ein Buch.
items.sentence_translation: Every evening in bed she reads a book.
items.grammar_tip: 'Lesen' is an irregular verb changing e to ie.

items.sentence_de: Sie haben heute einen Termin beim Arzt, Herr Müller.
items.sentence_translation: You have an appointment with the doctor, Mr. Müller.
items.grammar_tip: Formal 'Sie' always takes the infinitive verb form.

items.sentence_de: Guten Tag, Sie sind sicher Frau Schmidt, richtig?
items.sentence_translation: Good day, you are surely Ms. Schmidt, right?
items.grammar_tip: 'Sind' is the plural and formal form of 'sein'.

items.sentence_de: Eine Woche hat genau sieben Tage für uns.
items.sentence_translation: A week has exactly seven days for us.
items.grammar_tip: 'Sieben' is the number after six.

items.sentence_de: Der Unterricht beginnt morgen um acht Uhr pünktlich.
items.sentence_translation: The class starts tomorrow at eight o'clock sharp.
items.grammar_tip: Use 'um' to indicate a specific time of day.

items.sentence_de: Können Sie uns bitte den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
items.sentence_translation: Can you please show us the way to the station?
items.grammar_tip: 'Uns' is the accusative/dative pronoun for 'wir'.

items.sentence_de: Mein Auto hat vier Türen und fünf Plätze.
items.sentence_translation: My car has four doors and five seats.
items.grammar_tip: 'Vier' is the number after three.

items.sentence_de: Es ist jetzt genau Viertel nach acht Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: It is exactly quarter past eight now.
items.grammar_tip: 'Viertel nach' means 15 minutes past the hour.

items.sentence_de: Wir treffen uns um Viertel vor neun Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: We are meeting at quarter to nine.
items.grammar_tip: 'Viertel vor' means 15 minutes before the hour.

items.sentence_de: Entschuldigung, Wie spät ist es bitte gerade genau?
items.sentence_translation: Excuse me, what time is it exactly right now?
items.grammar_tip: A standard phrase to ask for the current time.

items.sentence_de: Sagen Sie mir bitte, wie viel das kostet.
items.sentence_translation: Please tell me how much that costs.
items.grammar_tip: 'Wie viel' asks about uncountable quantities or price.

items.sentence_de: Heute wir haben leider sehr viel Arbeit vor.
items.sentence_translation: Unfortunately, we have a lot of work today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Haben' matches with 'wir' in the plural form.

items.sentence_de: Wir sind seit fünf Jahren eine glückliche Familie.
items.sentence_translation: We have been a happy family for five years.
items.grammar_tip: 'Sind' is the first person plural of 'sein'.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte bitte zehn Eier im Supermarkt kaufen.
items.sentence_translation: I would like to buy ten eggs at the supermarket.
items.grammar_tip: 'Zehn' is the number after nine.

items.sentence_de: Das Ticket für den Bus kostet heute zwanzig Euro.
items.sentence_translation: The bus ticket costs twenty euros today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Zwanzig' is 20 in German.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe zwei kleine Brüder.
items.sentence_translation: I have two little brothers.
items.grammar_tip: Numbers do not change for gender in basic counting.

items.sentence_de: Es ist jetzt genau zwölf Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: It is exactly twelve o'clock now.
items.grammar_tip: Numbers 11 and 12 are irregular in German.

items.sentence_de: Nennen Sie alle Zahlen ab zwanzig.
items.sentence_translation: Name all numbers starting at twenty.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ab' is used for starting points in time or sequences.

items.sentence_de: Ich arbeite viel, aber ich habe frei.
items.sentence_translation: I work a lot, but I am free.
items.grammar_tip: 'Aber' is a coordinating conjunction and does not change word order.

items.sentence_de: Wann ist die Abfahrt nach Berlin?
items.sentence_translation: When is the departure to Berlin?
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in -fahrt are always feminine (die).

items.sentence_de: Ich muss mein Paket bei der Post abholen.
items.sentence_translation: I have to pick up my package at the post office.
items.grammar_tip: 'Abholen' is a separable verb (ich hole ab).

items.sentence_de: Der Absender steht oben links auf dem Brief.
items.sentence_translation: The sender is at the top left of the letter.
items.grammar_tip: Masculine nouns ending in -er often have the same plural form.

items.sentence_de: Wie ist deine neue Adresse in Wien?
items.sentence_translation: What is your new address in Vienna?
items.grammar_tip: Feminine nouns ending in -e usually add -n in plural.

items.sentence_de: Ich lebe nicht gern ganz allein zu Hause.
items.sentence_translation: I don't like living all alone at home.
items.grammar_tip: 'Allein' can be an adjective or an adverb.

items.sentence_de: Kein Bus fährt, also gehen wir schnell!
items.sentence_translation: No bus is running, so let's go quickly!
items.grammar_tip: 'Also' often starts a logical consequence.

items.sentence_de: Ich bin zweiundzwanzig Jahre alt.
items.sentence_translation: I am twenty-two years old.
items.grammar_tip: German uses 'alt sein' to express age.

items.sentence_de: Bitte geben Sie Ihr Alter im Formular an.
items.sentence_translation: Please state your age on the form.
items.grammar_tip: This is a neuter noun (das).

items.sentence_de: An jedem Wochenende kommen viele Fans.
items.sentence_translation: Every weekend, many fans come.
items.grammar_tip: 'An' is a two-way preposition, here used with time.

items.sentence_de: Der Kurs beginnt am Anfang des Monats.
items.sentence_translation: The course begins at the beginning of the month.
items.grammar_tip: 'Am Anfang' is a common fixed temporal expression.

items.sentence_de: Das ist ein sehr gutes Angebot heute.
items.sentence_translation: That is a very good offer today.
items.grammar_tip: Neuter noun; the plural is formed by adding -e.

items.sentence_de: Bitte kreuzen Sie die richtige Antwort an.
items.sentence_translation: Please mark the correct answer.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ankreuzen' is a separable verb (ich kreuze an).

items.sentence_de: Die Ankunft des Zuges ist um acht Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: The arrival of the train is at eight o'clock.
items.grammar_tip: Feminine noun; opposite of 'Abfahrt'.

items.sentence_de: Können Sie bitte das Licht anmachen?
items.sentence_translation: Can you please turn on the light?
items.grammar_tip: A separable verb used for electronic devices or lights.

items.sentence_de: Wo bekomme ich das Formular für die Anmeldung?
items.sentence_translation: Where do I get the form for the application?
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine.

items.sentence_de: Wählen Sie eine passende Anrede für den Brief.
items.sentence_translation: Choose a suitable salutation for the letter.
items.grammar_tip: Refers to titles like 'Herr' or 'Frau' in correspondence.

items.sentence_de: Vielen Dank für Ihren Anruf heute Morgen.
items.sentence_translation: Thank you for your call this morning.
items.grammar_tip: Masculine noun related to the verb 'anrufen'.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte meine Mutter am Abend anrufen.
items.sentence_translation: I want to call my mother in the evening.
items.grammar_tip: Separable verb; takes the accusative case.

items.sentence_de: Habe ich in Frankfurt einen Anschluss nach Köln?
items.sentence_translation: Do I have a connection to Cologne in Frankfurt?
items.grammar_tip: Commonly used for trains, buses, and internet.

items.sentence_de: Ich warte auf eine Antwort von Ihnen.
items.sentence_translation: I am waiting for an answer from you.
items.grammar_tip: Feminine noun; often used with the preposition 'auf'.

items.sentence_de: Bitte antworten Sie mir so schnell wie möglich.
items.sentence_translation: Please answer me as soon as possible.
items.grammar_tip: The verb 'antworten' takes the dative case for the person.

items.sentence_de: Ich lese eine Anzeige für eine Wohnung.
items.sentence_translation: I am reading an advertisement for an apartment.
items.grammar_tip: The noun Anzeige is feminine and uses the article die.

items.sentence_de: Das neue Apartment ist klein aber modern.
items.sentence_translation: The new apartment is small but modern.
items.grammar_tip: Loanwords like Apartment often take the neuter article das.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse jeden Morgen einen roten Apfel.
items.sentence_translation: I eat a red apple every morning.
items.grammar_tip: Der Apfel is a masculine noun ending in -el.

items.sentence_de: Meine Arbeit im Büro macht viel Spaß.
items.sentence_translation: My work in the office is a lot of fun.
items.grammar_tip: Die Arbeit is feminine and refers to general labor or employment.

items.sentence_de: Wir arbeiten heute zusammen in einem Team.
items.sentence_translation: We are working together in a team today.
items.grammar_tip: The verb arbeiten requires an extra -e- in some conjugations (du arbeitest).

items.sentence_de: Mein Bruder ist seit zwei Monaten arbeitslos.
items.sentence_translation: My brother has been unemployed for two months.
items.grammar_tip: Adjectives like arbeitslos are not capitalized unless at the start.

items.sentence_de: Mein linker Arm tut nach dem Sport weh.
items.sentence_translation: My left arm hurts after exercising.
items.grammar_tip: Der Arm is masculine and has a simple plural form.

items.sentence_de: Ich komme aus Berlin und Paul auch.
items.sentence_translation: I come from Berlin and Paul does too.
items.grammar_tip: Auch is an adverb used to express similarity or addition.

items.sentence_de: Wie heißt das Wort auf Deutsch?
items.sentence_translation: What is that word called in German?
items.grammar_tip: Use auf when referring to languages or being on top of something.

items.sentence_de: Das Fenster muss in der Nacht auf sein.
items.sentence_translation: The window must be open at night.
items.grammar_tip: Auf sein is a separable phrase meaning to be open.

items.sentence_de: Sie hat ein blaues und ein grünes Auge.
items.sentence_translation: She has one blue and one green eye.
items.grammar_tip: Das Auge is neuter and ends in -n in the plural.

items.sentence_de: Ich komme ursprünglich aus der Schweiz.
items.sentence_translation: I am originally from Switzerland.
items.grammar_tip: Aus is a dative preposition used for origins and materials.

items.sentence_de: Wir machen am Wochenende einen Ausflug.
items.sentence_translation: We are going on an excursion this weekend.
items.grammar_tip: Der Ausflug is masculine and often used with the verb machen.

items.sentence_de: Wo ist der Ausgang in diesem Bahnhof?
items.sentence_translation: Where is the exit in this train station?
items.grammar_tip: Ausgang is masculine and related to the verb ausgehen.

items.sentence_de: Er möchte ein Jahr im Ausland leben.
items.sentence_translation: He wants to live abroad for a year.
items.grammar_tip: Das Ausland is a neuter singular noun meaning foreign countries.

items.sentence_de: Können Sie bitte das Licht ausmachen?
items.sentence_translation: Can you please turn off the light?
items.grammar_tip: Ausmachen is a separable verb (ich mache das Licht aus).

items.sentence_de: Ist diese Aussage richtig oder falsch?
items.sentence_translation: Is this statement true or false?
items.grammar_tip: Die Aussage is feminine and ends in -e.

items.sentence_de: Haben Sie Ihren Ausweis dabei?
items.sentence_translation: Do you have your ID card with you?
items.grammar_tip: Der Ausweis is masculine and refers to any identification document.

items.sentence_de: Mein Vater kauft sich ein neues Auto.
items.sentence_translation: My father is buying himself a new car.
items.grammar_tip: Das Auto is neuter and takes an -s for the plural.

items.sentence_de: Wir fahren heute schnell auf der Autobahn.
items.sentence_translation: We are driving fast on the highway today.
items.grammar_tip: Die Autobahn is feminine; note the compound of Auto and Bahn.

items.sentence_de: Der Automat am Bahnhof ist leider kaputt.
items.sentence_translation: The vending machine at the station is unfortunately broken.
items.grammar_tip: Der Automat is a masculine n-declension noun.

items.sentence_de: Das Baby schläft sehr viel am Tag.
items.sentence_translation: The baby sleeps a lot during the day.
items.grammar_tip: Das Baby is neuter and uses the English-style plural -s.

items.sentence_de: Ich kaufe frisches Brot in der Bäckerei.
items.sentence_translation: I buy fresh bread at the bakery.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in -ei are always feminine.

items.sentence_de: Ich nehme am Abend ein warmes Bad.
items.sentence_translation: I take a warm bath in the evening.
items.grammar_tip: Das Bad is neuter and can refer to the bath or the bathroom.

items.sentence_de: Die Kinder baden im Sommer gerne im See.
items.sentence_translation: The children like to swim/bathe in the lake in summer.
items.grammar_tip: Baden is a regular verb often used for swimming in lakes/seas.

items.sentence_de: Ich fahre jetzt zum großen Bahnhof.
items.sentence_translation: I am driving to the big train station now.
items.grammar_tip: The noun 'Bahnhof' is masculine and takes 'der'.

items.sentence_de: Der Zug steht an dem Bahnsteig neun.
items.sentence_translation: The train is at platform nine.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bahnsteig' refers to the specific platform area in a station.

items.sentence_de: Der Film im Kino beginnt bald.
items.sentence_translation: The film at the cinema starts soon.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bald' is an adverb used to indicate a short time from now.

items.sentence_de: Meine neue Wohnung hat einen kleinen Balkon.
items.sentence_translation: My new apartment has a small balcony.
items.grammar_tip: 'Balkon' is masculine and uses the 'der' article.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse zum Frühstück eine gelbe Banane.
items.sentence_translation: I am eating a yellow banana for breakfast.
items.grammar_tip: Fruit names ending in -e are often feminine.

items.sentence_de: Wir sitzen im Park auf einer Bank.
items.sentence_translation: We are sitting on a bench in the park.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bank' can mean bench or bank institution; context determines meaning.

items.sentence_de: Können wir im Restaurant bitte bar bezahlen?
items.sentence_translation: Can we please pay in cash at the restaurant?
items.grammar_tip: 'Bar' is used without an article when referring to payment.

items.sentence_de: Trinken wir ein Bier in der Bar?
items.sentence_translation: Are we drinking a beer in the bar?
items.grammar_tip: The feminine noun 'Bar' refers to a drinking establishment.

items.sentence_de: Mein Bauch tut mir heute sehr weh.
items.sentence_translation: My stomach hurts a lot today.
items.grammar_tip: Body parts like 'Bauch' are usually masculine.

items.sentence_de: Was soll das Wort auf Deutsch bedeuten?
items.sentence_translation: What is that word supposed to mean in German?
items.grammar_tip: 'Bedeuten' is used to ask for the meaning of symbols or words.

items.sentence_de: Wir beginnen morgen mit dem neuen Kurs.
items.sentence_translation: We begin the new course tomorrow.
items.grammar_tip: 'Beginnen' is a strong verb that means to start.

items.sentence_de: Ich arbeite seit Januar bei Taxi-Zentral.
items.sentence_translation: I have been working at Taxi-Zentral since January.
items.grammar_tip: The preposition 'bei' always takes the dative case.

items.sentence_de: Sind beide Kinder schon in der Schule?
items.sentence_translation: Are both children already in school?
items.grammar_tip: 'Beide' refers to two specific things or people.

items.sentence_de: Mein rechtes Bein ist vom Laufen müde.
items.sentence_translation: My right leg is tired from running.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bein' is a neuter noun taking 'das'.

items.sentence_de: Nennen Sie mir bitte ein kurzes Beispiel.
items.sentence_translation: Please give me a short example.
items.grammar_tip: The phrase 'zum Beispiel' is very common for 'for example'.

items.sentence_de: Dieser Musiker ist in Deutschland sehr bekannt.
items.sentence_translation: This musician is very well-known in Germany.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bekannt' is an adjective used to describe fame or familiarity.

items.sentence_de: Sie benutzen den Computer für die Arbeit.
items.sentence_translation: They use the computer for work.
items.grammar_tip: 'Benutzen' is a regular verb meaning to utilize something.

items.sentence_de: Was sind Sie eigentlich von Beruf?
items.sentence_translation: What is your occupation, actually?
items.grammar_tip: When asking about jobs, use the phrase 'von Beruf'.

items.sentence_de: Das Telefon ist schon die ganze Zeit besetzt.
items.sentence_translation: The telephone has been busy the whole time.
items.grammar_tip: 'Besetzt' means occupied or busy in terms of lines or seats.

items.sentence_de: Wir besichtigen morgen das alte Schloss.
items.sentence_translation: We are visiting/viewing the old castle tomorrow.
items.grammar_tip: 'Besichtigen' is used for sightseeing or viewing buildings.

items.sentence_de: Mein Deutsch ist heute viel besser.
items.sentence_translation: My German is much better today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Besser' is the comparative form of the adjective 'gut'.

items.sentence_de: Wir möchten jetzt gern das Essen bestellen.
items.sentence_translation: We would like to order the food now.
items.grammar_tip: Use 'bestellen' when asking for food or goods in a shop.

items.sentence_de: Am Sonntag besuchen wir meine Großeltern.
items.sentence_translation: On Sunday we are visiting my grandparents.
items.grammar_tip: 'Besuchen' is used for visiting people or cultural places.

items.sentence_de: Das Kind liegt schon lange im Bett.
items.sentence_translation: The child has been in bed for a long time.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bett' is a neuter noun and takes 'das'.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte bitte die Rechnung jetzt bezahlen.
items.sentence_translation: I would like to pay the bill now, please.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bezahlen' is a weak verb used for monetary transactions.

items.sentence_de: Das Bild an der Wand ist sehr schön.
items.sentence_translation: The picture on the wall is very beautiful.
items.grammar_tip: The noun 'Bild' is neuter.

items.sentence_de: Das T-Shirt ist im Angebot und sehr billig.
items.sentence_translation: The t-shirt is on sale and very cheap.
items.grammar_tip: 'billig' is an adjective meaning low-cost.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse zum Frühstück eine süße Birne.
items.sentence_translation: I am eating a sweet pear for breakfast.
items.grammar_tip: Most fruit names ending in -e are feminine.

items.sentence_de: Geben Sie mir bitte ein Glas Wasser.
items.sentence_translation: Please give me a glass of water.
items.grammar_tip: 'bitte' is used for requests and 'you're welcome'.

items.sentence_de: Haben Sie einen Bleistift für die Notizen?
items.sentence_translation: Do you have a pencil for the notes?
items.grammar_tip: 'Bleistift' is a masculine compound noun.

items.sentence_de: Das Hotelzimmer hat einen tollen Blick.
items.sentence_translation: The hotel room has a great view.
items.grammar_tip: 'Blick' refers to a sight or glance.

items.sentence_de: Diese gelbe Blume riecht wirklich sehr gut.
items.sentence_translation: This yellow flower smells really very good.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in -e are frequently feminine.

items.sentence_de: Warum bist du heute so böse auf mich?
items.sentence_translation: Why are you so angry at me today?
items.grammar_tip: 'böse' describes a negative mood or character.

items.sentence_de: Wir brauchen Hilfe bei der Arbeit im Büro.
items.sentence_translation: We need help with the work in the office.
items.grammar_tip: 'brauchen' is a regular verb requiring an accusative object.

items.sentence_de: Die Straße in der Stadt ist sehr breit.
items.sentence_translation: The street in the city is very wide.
items.grammar_tip: 'breit' is the opposite of 'schmal'.

items.sentence_de: Ich schreibe heute einen Brief an meine Oma.
items.sentence_translation: I am writing a letter to my grandma today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Brief' is a masculine noun.

items.sentence_de: Das frische Brot vom Bäcker schmeckt lecker.
items.sentence_translation: The fresh bread from the baker tastes delicious.
items.grammar_tip: 'Brot' is a neuter noun.

items.sentence_de: Möchtest du zum Frühstück ein Brötchen essen?
items.sentence_translation: Would you like to eat a roll for breakfast?
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in -chen are always neuter.

items.sentence_de: Mein kleiner Bruder geht noch zur Schule.
items.sentence_translation: My little brother is still going to school.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bruder' takes an umlaut in its plural form.

items.sentence_de: Wie heißt der erste Buchstabe von Ihrem Namen?
items.sentence_translation: What is the first letter of your name?
items.grammar_tip: 'Buchstabe' is a masculine noun following the n-declension.

items.sentence_de: Können Sie bitte Ihren Namen langsam buchstabieren?
items.sentence_translation: Can you please spell your name slowly?
items.grammar_tip: Verbs ending in -ieren follow a regular pattern.

items.sentence_de: Ich fahre jeden Morgen mit dem Bus.
items.sentence_translation: I go by bus every morning.
items.grammar_tip: 'Bus' is masculine and often used with 'mit'.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse mein Brot am liebsten mit Butter.
items.sentence_translation: I like my bread best with butter.
items.grammar_tip: 'Butter' is feminine in German.

items.sentence_de: Wir treffen uns um drei Uhr im Café.
items.sentence_translation: We are meeting at three o'clock in the café.
items.grammar_tip: 'Café' is neuter and refers to the establishment.

items.sentence_de: Hörst du noch Musik von einer alten CD?
items.sentence_translation: Do you still listen to music from an old CD?
items.grammar_tip: Abbreviated nouns like 'CD' often take the feminine gender.

items.sentence_de: Mein Chef ist heute sehr zufrieden mit mir.
items.sentence_translation: My boss is very satisfied with me today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Chef' refers to a superior at work.

items.sentence_de: Ich arbeite den ganzen Tag am Computer.
items.sentence_translation: I work on the computer all day.
items.grammar_tip: The plural form of 'Computer' remains the same.

items.sentence_de: Dort steht der Tisch, und da ist mein Stuhl.
items.sentence_translation: The table is over there, and there is my chair.
items.grammar_tip: 'da' is an adverb indicating a location.

items.sentence_de: Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, guten Tag.
items.sentence_translation: Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, good day.
items.grammar_tip: 'Dame' is feminine and formal.

items.sentence_de: Hier ist die Post und direkt daneben ist die Bank.
items.sentence_translation: Here is the post office and right beside it is the bank.
items.grammar_tip: 'daneben' is a pronominal adverb of place.

items.sentence_de: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe.
items.sentence_translation: Many thanks for your help.
items.grammar_tip: 'Vielen Dank' is a fixed accusative expression used for expressing gratitude.

items.sentence_de: Ich danke Ihnen sehr herzlich.
items.sentence_translation: I thank you very much.
items.grammar_tip: 'Danke' can be a verb form or a simple interjection.

items.sentence_de: Wir danken dir für das Geschenk.
items.sentence_translation: We thank you for the gift.
items.grammar_tip: The verb 'danken' always takes the dative case for the person being thanked.

items.sentence_de: Zuerst essen wir, dann gehen wir.
items.sentence_translation: First we eat, then we go.
items.grammar_tip: 'Dann' is a temporal adverb often used to sequence events.

items.sentence_de: Wie lange wird die Reise dauern?
items.sentence_translation: How long will the journey last?
items.grammar_tip: Use 'dauern' to talk about the duration of time.

items.sentence_de: Was ist denn heute hier los?
items.sentence_translation: What is going on here then?
items.grammar_tip: As a particle, 'denn' adds a tone of curiosity to questions.

items.sentence_de: Wie geht es dir heute?
items.sentence_translation: How are you today?
items.grammar_tip: 'Dir' is the dative form of the informal 'du'.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte ein Doppelzimmer mit Bad.
items.sentence_translation: I would like a twin room with a bath.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-zimmer' are always neuter (das).

items.sentence_de: Die Kinder spielen heute alle draußen.
items.sentence_translation: The children are all playing outside today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Draußen' refers to a location, not a direction.

items.sentence_de: Kannst du bitte das Dokument drucken?
items.sentence_translation: Can you please print the document?
items.grammar_tip: Don't confuse 'drucken' (to print) with 'drücken' (to press).

items.sentence_de: Der neue Drucker im Büro funktioniert.
items.sentence_translation: The new printer in the office works.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns for tools ending in '-er' are usually masculine.

items.sentence_de: Wir gehen direkt durch den Park.
items.sentence_translation: We are going directly through the park.
items.grammar_tip: The preposition 'durch' always requires the accusative case.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe nach dem Sport Durst.
items.sentence_translation: I am thirsty after sports.
items.grammar_tip: In German, you 'have' thirst ('Ich habe Durst') rather than 'being' thirsty.

items.sentence_de: Die Dusche ist im Badezimmer links.
items.sentence_translation: The shower is in the bathroom on the left.
items.grammar_tip: Most German nouns ending in '-e' are feminine.

items.sentence_de: Schreiben Sie mir bitte eine E-Mail.
items.sentence_translation: Please write me an e-mail.
items.grammar_tip: 'E-Mail' is feminine (die) in German.

items.sentence_de: Das Restaurant ist an der Ecke.
items.sentence_translation: The restaurant is on the corner.
items.grammar_tip: 'An der Ecke' uses the dative case because it describes a location.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse zum Frühstück ein Ei.
items.sentence_translation: I eat an egg for breakfast.
items.grammar_tip: The plural of 'Ei' is 'Eier'.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe es heute sehr eilig.
items.sentence_translation: I am in a great hurry today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Es eilig haben' is a common idiom for being in a hurry.

items.sentence_de: Die Hausaufgabe ist wirklich sehr einfach.
items.sentence_translation: The homework is really very easy.
items.grammar_tip: 'Einfach' can mean both 'easy' and 'simple'.

items.sentence_de: Ich gehe jeden Samstag im Supermarkt einkaufen.
items.sentence_translation: I go shopping at the supermarket every Saturday.
items.grammar_tip: 'Einkaufen' is a separable verb: 'Ich kaufe heute ein.'

items.sentence_de: Danke für die Einladung zur Party.
items.sentence_translation: Thanks for the invitation to the party.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-ung' are always feminine.

items.sentence_de: Ich war erst einmal in Berlin.
items.sentence_translation: I have only been to Berlin once.
items.grammar_tip: 'Einmal' combines the number 'eins' with the suffix '-mal' for frequency.

items.sentence_de: Der Eintritt für das Museum kostet nichts.
items.sentence_translation: Admission to the museum costs nothing.
items.grammar_tip: 'Eintritt' usually refers to the price or right of entering.

items.sentence_de: Haben Sie noch ein freies Einzelzimmer?
items.sentence_translation: Do you still have a free single room?
items.grammar_tip: Like 'Doppelzimmer', this noun is neuter.

items.sentence_de: Meine Eltern wohnen in einem Dorf.
items.sentence_translation: My parents live in a village.
items.grammar_tip: 'Eltern' is a plural-only noun in common usage.

items.sentence_de: Der Name vom Empfänger steht hier.
items.sentence_translation: The recipient's name is written here.
items.grammar_tip: 'Empfänger' comes from the verb 'empfangen' (to receive).

items.sentence_de: Der Film ist am Ende traurig.
items.sentence_translation: The movie is sad at the end.
items.grammar_tip: 'Am Ende' is the standard phrase for 'at the end'.

items.sentence_de: Wann wird der Kurs endlich enden?
items.sentence_translation: When will the course finally end?
items.grammar_tip: 'Enden' is an intransitive verb (it doesn't take a direct object).

items.sentence_de: Bitte entschuldigen Sie die kurze Verspätung.
items.sentence_translation: Please excuse the short delay.
items.grammar_tip: This is the formal imperative form used to apologize.

items.sentence_de: Entschuldigung, wo ist der Bahnhof, bitte?
items.sentence_translation: Excuse me, where is the train station, please?
items.grammar_tip: Use this word to get someone's attention or apologize.

items.sentence_de: Das Ergebnis der Prüfung war gut.
items.sentence_translation: The result of the exam was good.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-nis' are often neuter and add '-se' in plural.

items.sentence_de: Können Sie mir die Regel erklären?
items.sentence_translation: Can you explain the rule to me?
items.grammar_tip: 'Erklären' is a weak verb and does not have a separable prefix.

items.sentence_de: Opa kann sehr gute Geschichten erzählen.
items.sentence_translation: Grandpa can tell very good stories.
items.grammar_tip: 'Erzählen' implies a longer narrative than 'sagen'.

items.sentence_de: Das Essen im Restaurant schmeckt prima.
items.sentence_translation: The food in the restaurant tastes great.
items.grammar_tip: In German, verbs can become neuter nouns (das Essen).

items.sentence_de: Ich muss noch eine Fahrkarte kaufen.
items.sentence_translation: I still have to buy a ticket.
items.grammar_tip: 'Fahrkarte' is specifically for travel; 'Ticket' is also common.

items.sentence_de: Das ist leider die falsche Nummer.
items.sentence_translation: Unfortunately, that is the wrong number.
items.grammar_tip: 'Falsch' is the opposite of 'richtig'.

items.sentence_de: Meine Familie kommt aus der Schweiz.
items.sentence_translation: My family comes from Switzerland.
items.grammar_tip: The word 'Familie' is singular even though it refers to multiple people.

items.sentence_de: Mein Familienname ist schwer zu buchstabieren.
items.sentence_translation: My surname is difficult to spell.
items.grammar_tip: 'Nachname' is a common synonym for 'Familienname'.

items.sentence_de: Welche Farbe hat dein neues Auto?
items.sentence_translation: What color is your new car?
items.grammar_tip: 'Farbe' is feminine; plural ends in '-n'.

items.sentence_de: In dem Satz fehlen zwei Wörter.
items.sentence_translation: Two words are missing in the sentence.
items.grammar_tip: 'Fehlen' can also mean to be absent from school/work.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe viele Fehler im Test.
items.sentence_translation: I have many mistakes in the test.
items.grammar_tip: The singular and plural forms of 'Fehler' are the same.

items.sentence_de: Wir feiern morgen meinen 30. Geburtstag.
items.sentence_translation: We are celebrating my 30th birthday tomorrow.
items.grammar_tip: 'Feiern' is a regular weak verb.

items.sentence_de: Heute Abend gibt es nichts im Fernsehen.
items.sentence_translation: There is nothing on TV tonight.
items.grammar_tip: 'Fernsehen' is the activity/medium; 'Fernseher' is the physical device.

items.sentence_de: Bist du mit deinen Hausaufgaben fertig?
items.sentence_translation: Are you finished with your homework?
items.grammar_tip: 'Fertig' is usually followed by the preposition 'mit'.

items.sentence_de: Das Kind hat leider sehr hohes Fieber.
items.sentence_translation: The child unfortunately has a very high fever.
items.grammar_tip: Fever is 'neuter' (das) in German.

items.sentence_de: Der Film beginnt um acht Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: The movie starts at eight o'clock.
items.grammar_tip: The plural of 'Film' is 'Filme'.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse gerne Fisch mit Reis.
items.sentence_translation: I like eating fish with rice.
items.grammar_tip: Like most animals used for food, 'Fisch' is masculine.

items.sentence_de: Bringen Sie uns eine Flasche Wasser?
items.sentence_translation: Will you bring us a bottle of water?
items.grammar_tip: 'Flasche' is feminine.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse seit Jahren kein Fleisch mehr.
items.sentence_translation: I haven't eaten meat for years.
items.grammar_tip: 'Fleisch' is an uncountable noun in this context.

items.sentence_de: Wie komme ich zum Flughafen Berlin?
items.sentence_translation: How do I get to Berlin airport?
items.grammar_tip: A compound of 'Flug' (flight) and 'Hafen' (port).

items.sentence_de: Das Flugzeug landet in zehn Minuten.
items.sentence_translation: The airplane lands in ten minutes.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-zeug' (tool/thing) are always neuter.

items.sentence_de: Füllen Sie bitte dieses Formular aus.
items.sentence_translation: Please fill out this form.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ausfüllen' is the verb commonly used with 'Formular'.

items.sentence_de: Darf ich hier ein Foto machen?
items.sentence_translation: May I take a photo here?
items.grammar_tip: The plural of 'Foto' is 'Fotos'.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe eine Frage zum Unterricht.
items.sentence_translation: I have a question about the lesson.
items.grammar_tip: The verb is 'fragen', the noun is 'die Frage'.

items.sentence_de: Darf ich Sie etwas Persönliches fragen?
items.sentence_translation: May I ask you something personal?
items.grammar_tip: 'Fragen' takes an accusative object for the person being asked.

items.sentence_de: Frau Müller ist meine neue Lehrerin.
items.sentence_translation: Mrs. Müller is my new teacher.
items.grammar_tip: Use 'Frau' as a title for all adult women.

items.sentence_de: Ist dieser Platz hier noch frei?
items.sentence_translation: Is this seat here still free?
items.grammar_tip: 'Frei' can mean 'vacant' (seats) or 'free of charge'.

items.sentence_de: Was machst du in deiner Freizeit?
items.sentence_translation: What do you do in your free time?
items.grammar_tip: 'Zeit' nouns are almost always feminine.

items.sentence_de: Mein Freund kommt aus den USA.
items.sentence_translation: My friend comes from the USA.
items.grammar_tip: 'Freund' can mean 'friend' or 'boyfriend'.

items.sentence_de: Früher gab es hier keinen Supermarkt.
items.sentence_translation: In the past, there was no supermarket here.
items.grammar_tip: 'Früher' is the comparative of 'früh' (early).

items.sentence_de: Das Frühstück ist die wichtigste Mahlzeit.
items.sentence_translation: Breakfast is the most important meal.
items.grammar_tip: Literally 'early piece'. It is always neuter.

items.sentence_de: Wir frühstücken meistens um sieben Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: We usually eat breakfast at seven o'clock.
items.grammar_tip: A verb derived directly from the noun 'Frühstück'.

items.sentence_de: Das Geschenk ist nur für dich.
items.sentence_translation: The gift is only for you.
items.grammar_tip: 'Für' is a preposition that always triggers the accusative case.

items.sentence_de: Wir grillen im Sommer oft im Garten.
items.sentence_translation: We often barbecue in the garden in summer.
items.grammar_tip: The plural 'Gärten' has an umlaut.

items.sentence_de: Kannst du mir bitte das Salz geben?
items.sentence_translation: Can you please give me the salt?
items.grammar_tip: 'Geben' is an irregular verb: ich gebe, du gibst, er gibt.

items.sentence_de: Schreiben Sie Ihren Geburtsort ins Formular.
items.sentence_translation: Write your place of birth on the form.
items.grammar_tip: A compound of 'Geburt' (birth) and 'Ort' (place).

items.sentence_de: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zu deinem Geburtstag!
items.sentence_translation: Happy birthday to you!
items.grammar_tip: 'Geburtstag' is masculine because 'Tag' is masculine.

items.sentence_de: Kannst du mir einen Gefallen tun?
items.sentence_translation: Can you do me a favor?
items.grammar_tip: 'Jemandem einen Gefallen tun' is a standard idiom.

items.sentence_de: Hast du ein Medikament gegen Kopfschmerzen?
items.sentence_translation: Do you have a medicine for headaches?
items.grammar_tip: 'Gegen' always takes the accusative case.

items.sentence_de: Meine Kinder gehen jeden Tag zur Schule.
items.sentence_translation: My children go to school every day.
items.grammar_tip: 'Gehen' usually refers to movement on foot.

items.sentence_de: Das Buch gehört mir nicht.
items.sentence_translation: The book does not belong to me.
items.grammar_tip: The verb 'gehören' requires the dative case.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe leider kein Geld dabei.
items.sentence_translation: Unfortunately, I have no money with me.
items.grammar_tip: 'Geld' is neuter and often used in the singular.

items.sentence_de: Frisches Gemüse ist sehr gesund.
items.sentence_translation: Fresh vegetables are very healthy.
items.grammar_tip: 'Gemüse' is a collective noun and usually singular.

items.sentence_de: Der Supermarkt ist bis 20 Uhr geöffnet.
items.sentence_translation: The supermarket is open until 8 pm.
items.grammar_tip: 'Geöffnet' is the past participle of 'öffnen'.

items.sentence_de: Ich muss mein Gepäck am Schalter abgeben.
items.sentence_translation: I have to drop off my luggage at the counter.
items.grammar_tip: 'Gepäck' is a collective noun (das) and has no plural.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe gerade leider keine Zeit.
items.sentence_translation: I unfortunately have no time at the moment.
items.grammar_tip: 'Gerade' indicates that something is happening right now.

items.sentence_de: Das Geschäft hat heute leider geschlossen.
items.sentence_translation: The shop is unfortunately closed today.
items.grammar_tip: German nouns always start with a capital letter.

items.sentence_de: Das Geschenk ist für meine Mutter.
items.sentence_translation: The present is for my mother.
items.grammar_tip: The preposition 'für' is followed by the accusative case.

items.sentence_de: Die Bäckerei ist am Sonntag geschlossen.
items.sentence_translation: The bakery is closed on Sunday.
items.grammar_tip: 'Geschlossen' is often used for business opening hours.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe drei Geschwister: zwei Brüder.
items.sentence_translation: I have three siblings: two brothers.
items.grammar_tip: 'Geschwister' is a collective plural noun for brothers and sisters.

items.sentence_de: Das Gespräch mit dem Chef war gut.
items.sentence_translation: The conversation with the boss was good.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-gespräch' are always neuter.

items.sentence_de: Gestern war das Wetter sehr schön.
items.sentence_translation: Yesterday the weather was very beautiful.
items.grammar_tip: 'Gestern' triggers the past tense or past forms of 'sein'/'haben'.

items.sentence_de: Möchten Sie ein kaltes Getränk bestellen?
items.sentence_translation: Would you like to order a cold drink?
items.grammar_tip: Neuter nouns often end in '-k' in German.

items.sentence_de: Mein Gewicht ist seit einem Jahr gleich.
items.sentence_translation: My weight has been the same for a year.
items.grammar_tip: The prefix 'Ge-' often indicates a neuter noun.

items.sentence_de: Ich glaube, dass es morgen regnet.
items.sentence_translation: I believe that it will rain tomorrow.
items.grammar_tip: 'Glauben' is used for opinions or religious belief.

items.sentence_de: Das Essen ist in fünf Minuten gleich fertig.
items.sentence_translation: The food will be ready soon in five minutes.
items.grammar_tip: 'Gleich' means 'soon' or 'immediately' in a temporal context.

items.sentence_de: Der Zug fährt heute von Gleis acht.
items.sentence_translation: The train departs from track eight today.
items.grammar_tip: At the station, use 'von Gleis' (from track).

items.sentence_de: Viel Glück bei deiner Prüfung morgen!
items.sentence_translation: Good luck with your exam tomorrow!
items.grammar_tip: 'Viel Glück' is the standard way to wish someone luck.

items.sentence_de: Ich bin heute wirklich sehr glücklich.
items.sentence_translation: I am really very happy today.
items.grammar_tip: Adjectives in German don't change endings if they come after 'sein'.

items.sentence_de: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zu deinem neuen Job!
items.sentence_translation: Heartfelt congratulations on your new job!
items.grammar_tip: 'Glückwunsch' is usually used with the preposition 'zu'.

items.sentence_de: Wir grillen im Sommer oft im Garten.
items.sentence_translation: We often barbecue in the garden in summer.
items.grammar_tip: Regular -en verb conjugation: ich grille, du grillst, er grillt.

items.sentence_de: Die Wohnung ist für uns zu groß.
items.sentence_translation: The apartment is too large for us.
items.grammar_tip: The letter 'ß' (Eszett) follows a long vowel.

items.sentence_de: Welche Größe brauchen Sie für die Hose?
items.sentence_translation: What size do you need for the pants?
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-e' are very often feminine.

items.sentence_de: Meine Großeltern wohnen in einem kleinen Dorf.
items.sentence_translation: My grandparents live in a small village.
items.grammar_tip: This is a plural-only noun in common usage.

items.sentence_de: Meine Großmutter kocht am Sonntag für uns.
items.sentence_translation: My grandmother cooks for us on Sunday.
items.grammar_tip: 'Oma' is the common informal word for 'Großmutter'.

items.sentence_de: Mein Großvater geht jeden Morgen spazieren.
items.sentence_translation: My grandfather goes for a walk every morning.
items.grammar_tip: 'Opa' is the common informal word for 'Großvater'.

items.sentence_de: Wir lernen Deutsch in einer kleinen Gruppe.
items.sentence_translation: We learn German in a small group.
items.grammar_tip: Dative case 'in einer... Gruppe' because it describes location.

items.sentence_de: Dieses Hotel ist sehr gut und günstig.
items.sentence_translation: This hotel is very good and low-priced.
items.grammar_tip: 'Günstig' is a more positive word for 'billig' (cheap).

items.sentence_de: Guten Tag, wie geht es Ihnen heute?
items.sentence_translation: Good day, how are you today?
items.grammar_tip: Adjectives change endings when they precede a noun.

items.sentence_de: Sie hat langes, blondes Haar und blaue Augen.
items.sentence_translation: She has long, blonde hair and blue eyes.
items.grammar_tip: Usually used in singular 'das Haar' to refer to the whole head of hair.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte gerne einen Termin haben.
items.sentence_translation: I would like to have an appointment.
items.grammar_tip: 'Haben' takes the accusative case (einen Termin).

items.sentence_de: Ich esse heute Reis mit Hähnchen.
items.sentence_translation: I am eating rice with chicken today.
items.grammar_tip: Diminutives ending in '-chen' are always neuter.

items.sentence_de: Hallo Maria, wie geht es dir?
items.sentence_translation: Hello Maria, how are you?
items.grammar_tip: 'Hallo' is the universal informal greeting in German.

items.sentence_de: Wo ist die nächste Haltestelle für den Bus?
items.sentence_translation: Where is the next station for the bus?
items.grammar_tip: Specifically used for bus or tram stops.

items.sentence_de: Ich muss noch meine Hausaufgabe für morgen machen.
items.sentence_translation: I still have to do my homework for tomorrow.
items.grammar_tip: Often used in the plural: 'Hausaufgaben'.

items.sentence_de: Spanien ist meine Heimat, aber ich lebe hier.
items.sentence_translation: Spain is my home, but I live here.
items.grammar_tip: 'Heimat' refers to one's homeland or place of origin.

items.sentence_de: Das Wohnzimmer ist durch die Fenster sehr hell.
items.sentence_translation: The living room is very light because of the windows.
items.grammar_tip: 'Hell' is the opposite of 'dunkel' (dark).

items.sentence_de: Der Herd in der Küche ist neu.
items.sentence_translation: The stove in the kitchen is new.
items.grammar_tip: Household appliances often have the article 'der' or 'die'.

items.sentence_de: Wir gehen heute Abend ins Kino.
items.sentence_translation: We are going to the cinema tonight.
items.grammar_tip: Time adverbs like 'heute' usually come early in the sentence.

items.sentence_de: Ist hier noch ein Platz frei?
items.sentence_translation: Is a seat still free here?
items.grammar_tip: 'Hier' refers to the location of the speaker.

items.sentence_de: Ich brauche Hilfe bei dieser Aufgabe.
items.sentence_translation: I need help with this task.
items.grammar_tip: The verb form is 'helfen'.

items.sentence_de: Mein liebstes Hobby ist das Lesen.
items.sentence_translation: My favorite hobby is reading.
items.grammar_tip: German plural of 'Hobby' is 'Hobbys' (with 's', not 'ies').

items.sentence_de: Der Berg ist über dreitausend Meter hoch.
items.sentence_translation: The mountain is over three thousand meters high.
items.grammar_tip: The 'ch' sound is pronounced after 'o'.

items.sentence_de: Ich muss noch Geld bei der Bank holen.
items.sentence_translation: I still have to get money at the bank.
items.grammar_tip: 'Holen' means to go somewhere and bring something back.

items.sentence_de: Ich höre am Abend gerne Musik.
items.sentence_translation: I like to listen to music in the evening.
items.grammar_tip: 'Hören' means both 'to hear' and 'to listen'.

items.sentence_de: Wir suchen ein günstiges Hotel im Stadtzentrum.
items.sentence_translation: We are looking for a cheap hotel in the city center.
items.grammar_tip: International words in German are often neuter.

items.sentence_de: Mein Hund ist klein und sehr lieb.
items.sentence_translation: My dog is small and very sweet.
items.grammar_tip: Masculine animals often end in a consonant.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe großen Hunger, wann essen wir?
items.sentence_translation: I am very hungry, when are we eating?
items.grammar_tip: In German, you 'have' hunger (Ich habe Hunger).

items.sentence_de: Du bist immer so pünktlich bei der Arbeit.
items.sentence_translation: You are always so punctual at work.
items.grammar_tip: 'Immer' is the opposite of 'nie' (never).

items.sentence_de: Wie heißt das Wort in deiner Sprache?
items.sentence_translation: What is the word called in your language?
items.grammar_tip: 'In' takes the dative for location (where?) and accusative for direction.

items.sentence_de: Wo bekomme ich eine Information zum Zug?
items.sentence_translation: Where do I get information about the train?
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-tion' are always feminine.

items.sentence_de: An dieser Schule gibt es viele internationale Studenten.
items.sentence_translation: There are many international students at this school.
items.grammar_tip: This is a cognate, meaning it looks similar to English.

items.sentence_de: Gibt es hier im Zimmer freies Internet?
items.sentence_translation: Is there free internet here in the room?
items.grammar_tip: Usually used with the neuter article 'das'.

items.sentence_de: Liest du gerne? - Ja, sehr gerne.
items.sentence_translation: Do you like to read? - Yes, very much.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ja' is the standard affirmative answer.

items.sentence_de: Es ist kalt, zieh bitte deine Jacke an.
items.sentence_translation: It is cold, please put on your jacket.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-e' are mostly feminine.

items.sentence_de: Wir müssen jetzt gehen, der Bus kommt.
items.sentence_translation: We must go now, the bus is coming.
items.grammar_tip: 'Jetzt' refers to the immediate present.

items.sentence_de: Ich suche einen neuen Job als Kellner.
items.sentence_translation: I am looking for a new job as a waiter.
items.grammar_tip: 'Job' is a masculine loanword from English.

items.sentence_de: Mein Bruder ist noch sehr jung, erst fünf.
items.sentence_translation: My brother is still very young, only five.
items.grammar_tip: 'Jung' is the opposite of 'alt' (old).

items.sentence_de: Der Junge spielt mit seinem Ball im Park.
items.sentence_translation: The boy is playing with his ball in the park.
items.grammar_tip: 'Junge' is an n-declension noun: 'den Jungen'.

items.sentence_de: Trinken Sie Ihren Kaffee mit Milch und Zucker?
items.sentence_translation: Do you drink your coffee with milk and sugar?
items.grammar_tip: Most drinks ending in '-ee' or consonants are masculine.

items.sentence_de: Mein Fernseher ist leider seit gestern kaputt.
items.sentence_translation: My TV has unfortunately been broken since yesterday.
items.grammar_tip: Used for objects that don't work or are destroyed.

items.sentence_de: Kann ich mit Karte oder bar bezahlen?
items.sentence_translation: Can I pay by card or in cash?
items.grammar_tip: Can mean 'map', 'ticket', or 'credit card'.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse zum Abendessen Fleisch mit einer Kartoffel.
items.sentence_translation: I am eating meat with a potato for dinner.
items.grammar_tip: A staple food in Germany, always feminine.

items.sentence_de: Zahlen Sie bitte an der Kasse dort vorne.
items.sentence_translation: Please pay at the checkout over there.
items.grammar_tip: Also means 'cash register' or 'checkout'.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte heute ein neues Fahrrad kaufen.
items.sentence_translation: I would like to buy a new bicycle today.
items.grammar_tip: The opposite is 'verkaufen' (to sell).

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte neue Leute in der Stadt kennenlernen.
items.sentence_translation: I want to get to know new people in the city.
items.grammar_tip: This is a separable verb (Ich lerne dich kennen).

items.sentence_de: Das Kind schläft schon seit einer Stunde.
items.sentence_translation: The child has been sleeping for an hour.
items.grammar_tip: The plural is 'Kinder'.

items.sentence_de: Mein Sohn geht von Montag bis Freitag in den Kindergarten.
items.sentence_translation: My son goes to kindergarten from Monday to Friday.
items.grammar_tip: A compound noun: Kinder + Garten.

items.sentence_de: Gehen wir am Freitagabend zusammen ins Kino?
items.sentence_translation: Are we going to the movie theater together on Friday evening?
items.grammar_tip: Use 'ins' (in + das) for 'to the cinema'.

items.sentence_de: Kommst du mit? - Ja klar, gerne!
items.sentence_translation: Are you coming along? - Yes of course, gladly!
items.grammar_tip: 'Klar' is used to show agreement or certainty.

items.sentence_de: Im Winter brauche ich sehr warme Kleidung.
items.sentence_translation: In winter I need very warm clothes.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-ung' are always feminine.

items.sentence_de: Das Zimmer ist ein bisschen zu klein.
items.sentence_translation: The room is a bit too small.
items.grammar_tip: 'Klein' is the opposite of 'groß'.

items.sentence_de: Was kochen wir heute Abend zum Essen?
items.sentence_translation: What are we cooking for dinner tonight?
items.grammar_tip: Regular verb: ich koche, du kochst, er/sie/es kocht.

items.sentence_de: Der Koffer ist sehr schwer, hilf mir bitte.
items.sentence_translation: The suitcase is very heavy, help me please.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in '-er' are often masculine.

items.sentence_de: Mein Kollege hilft mir bei der Arbeit.
items.sentence_translation: My colleague helps me at work.
items.grammar_tip: The feminine form is 'die Kollegin'.

items.sentence_de: Mein Kopf tut weh, ich brauche eine Pause.
items.sentence_translation: My head hurts, I need a break.
items.grammar_tip: 'Kopfschmerzen' means headache.

items.sentence_de: Wie viel kosten die Äpfel pro Kilo?
items.sentence_translation: How much do the apples cost per kilo?
items.grammar_tip: Used with 'wie viel' to ask for prices.

items.sentence_de: Die Kosten für die Wohnung sind sehr hoch.
items.sentence_translation: The costs for the apartment are very high.
items.grammar_tip: This noun is used only in the plural.

items.sentence_de: Ich kann nicht arbeiten, ich bin leider krank.
items.sentence_translation: I cannot work, I am unfortunately sick.
items.grammar_tip: The opposite of 'krank' is 'gesund'.

items.sentence_de: Kriegen wir heute noch eine Antwort von Ihnen?
items.sentence_translation: Will we get an answer from you today?
items.grammar_tip: 'Kriegen' is more informal than 'bekommen'.

items.sentence_de: Meine neue Küche ist sehr groß.
items.sentence_translation: My new kitchen is very big.
items.grammar_tip: 'Küche' is a feminine noun; its plural is 'Küchen'.

items.sentence_de: Wir essen am Sonntag einen Kuchen.
items.sentence_translation: We are eating a cake on Sunday.
items.grammar_tip: 'Kuchen' is masculine and is often eaten during 'Kaffee und Kuchen'.

items.sentence_de: Haben Sie einen Kugelschreiber für mich?
items.sentence_translation: Do you have a ballpoint pen for me?
items.grammar_tip: Often shortened to 'Kuli' in everyday German conversation.

items.sentence_de: Die Milch steht im Kühlschrank.
items.sentence_translation: The milk is in the refrigerator.
items.grammar_tip: A compound word: 'kühlen' (to cool) + 'Schrank' (cupboard).

items.sentence_de: Der Kunde möchte bar bezahlen.
items.sentence_translation: The customer wants to pay in cash.
items.grammar_tip: This is an n-declension noun, so it adds -n in most cases.

items.sentence_de: Der Deutschkurs beginnt um neun Uhr.
items.sentence_translation: The German course starts at nine o'clock.
items.grammar_tip: 'Kurs' is masculine. Don't confuse it with 'Klasse'.

items.sentence_de: Schreiben Sie bitte einen kurzen Text.
items.sentence_translation: Please write a short text.
items.grammar_tip: Adjectives change endings based on the noun's gender and case.

items.sentence_de: Dieser Laden verkauft sehr schönes Obst.
items.sentence_translation: This shop sells very nice fruit.
items.grammar_tip: 'Laden' is masculine; the plural 'Läden' has an umlaut.

items.sentence_de: Der Film ist zwei Stunden lang.
items.sentence_translation: The movie is two hours long.
items.grammar_tip: 'Lang' describes duration or physical length.

items.sentence_de: Wir haben uns lange nicht gesehen.
items.sentence_translation: We haven't seen each other for a long time.
items.grammar_tip: Used here as an adverb to describe duration.

items.sentence_de: Fahren Sie bitte etwas langsamer.
items.sentence_translation: Please drive a bit slower.
items.grammar_tip: The opposite of 'langsam' is 'schnell'.

items.sentence_de: Die Musik ist mir zu laut.
items.sentence_translation: The music is too loud for me.
items.grammar_tip: 'Laut' can describe volume or noisy environments.

items.sentence_de: Das Leben in Berlin ist teuer.
items.sentence_translation: Life in Berlin is expensive.
items.grammar_tip: When used as a noun, 'Leben' is always neuter.

items.sentence_de: Ich kaufe heute viele Lebensmittel ein.
items.sentence_translation: I am buying many groceries today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Lebensmittel' is used as a collective plural for food items.

items.sentence_de: Sind Sie verheiratet oder ledig?
items.sentence_translation: Are you married or single?
items.grammar_tip: Commonly used on official forms regarding marital status.

items.sentence_de: Unser Lehrer kommt aus der Schweiz.
items.sentence_translation: Our teacher comes from Switzerland.
items.grammar_tip: The plural 'Lehrer' is the same as the singular.

items.sentence_de: Die Prüfung war eigentlich sehr leicht.
items.sentence_translation: The exam was actually very easy.
items.grammar_tip: 'Leicht' can mean both 'easy' and 'lightweight'.

items.sentence_de: Ich kann leider nicht zur Party kommen.
items.sentence_translation: Unfortunately, I cannot come to the party.
items.grammar_tip: 'Leider' is often used to soften a refusal or bad news.

items.sentence_de: Seid bitte leise, das Baby schläft.
items.sentence_translation: Please be quiet, the baby is sleeping.
items.grammar_tip: The opposite of 'leise' is 'laut'.

items.sentence_de: Sie lernt gerade Spanisch in Madrid.
items.sentence_translation: She is currently learning Spanish in Madrid.
items.grammar_tip: In German, 'lernen' is used for studying subjects or skills.

items.sentence_de: Hier sind heute sehr viele Leute.
items.sentence_translation: There are many people here today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Leute' is only used in the plural.

items.sentence_de: Mach bitte das Licht an, Schatz.
items.sentence_translation: Please turn on the light, honey.
items.grammar_tip: 'Licht' is neuter. The plural is 'Lichter'.

items.sentence_de: Ich liebe meine Familie über alles.
items.sentence_translation: I love my family above everything.
items.grammar_tip: Used for people, hobbies, or things you strongly like.

items.sentence_de: Singen wir zusammen ein schönes Lied?
items.sentence_translation: Shall we sing a beautiful song together?
items.grammar_tip: 'Lied' is neuter. The plural is 'Lieder'.

items.sentence_de: Gehen Sie an der Ecke links.
items.sentence_translation: Go left at the corner.
items.grammar_tip: Opposite of 'rechts'. Used for directions.

items.sentence_de: Das Lokal hat heute leider geschlossen.
items.sentence_translation: The restaurant is unfortunately closed today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Lokal' is a common word for a pub or restaurant.

items.sentence_de: Die Lösung für die Aufgabe fehlt.
items.sentence_translation: The solution for the task is missing.
items.grammar_tip: Feminine nouns ending in -ung take 'die' and plural -en.

items.sentence_de: Dein Onkel ist ein sehr lustiger Mann.
items.sentence_translation: Your uncle is a very funny man.
items.grammar_tip: 'Lustig' can mean funny or jovial.

items.sentence_de: Was machen Sie in Ihrer Freizeit?
items.sentence_translation: What do you do in your free time?
items.grammar_tip: 'Machen' is one of the most versatile verbs in German.

items.sentence_de: Das Mädchen spielt gern im Garten.
items.sentence_translation: The girl likes playing in the garden.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns with the suffix -chen are always neuter (das).

items.sentence_de: Hier darf man nicht laut sprechen.
items.sentence_translation: One is not allowed to speak loudly here.
items.grammar_tip: 'Man' refers to a general 'one' and takes 3rd person singular.

items.sentence_de: Bitte kreuzen Sie 'männlich' oder 'weiblich' an.
items.sentence_translation: Please mark 'male' or 'female'.
items.grammar_tip: Common on forms for identifying gender.

items.sentence_de: Wir machen Urlaub am Meer.
items.sentence_translation: We are going on holiday by the sea.
items.grammar_tip: 'Das Meer' usually refers to the ocean.

items.sentence_de: Wir haben keinen Käse mehr.
items.sentence_translation: We don't have any cheese anymore.
items.grammar_tip: 'Nicht mehr' or 'kein... mehr' means 'no longer/anymore'.

items.sentence_de: Jeder Mensch braucht Freunde im Leben.
items.sentence_translation: Every person needs friends in life.
items.grammar_tip: 'Mensch' refers to a human being. It is an n-declension noun.

items.sentence_de: Die Miete für die Wohnung ist hoch.
items.sentence_translation: The rent for the apartment is high.
items.grammar_tip: 'Miete' refers to the monthly payment for housing.

items.sentence_de: Trinken Sie Ihren Kaffee mit Milch?
items.sentence_translation: Do you drink your coffee with milk?
items.grammar_tip: 'Milch' is a feminine noun and usually used in the singular.

items.sentence_de: Kommst du mit mir ins Kino?
items.sentence_translation: Are you coming with me to the cinema?
items.grammar_tip: 'Mit' is a preposition that always requires the dative case.

items.sentence_de: Jeder kann bei diesem Spiel mitmachen.
items.sentence_translation: Everyone can participate in this game.
items.grammar_tip: 'Mitmachen' is a separable verb (ich mache mit).

items.sentence_de: Der Tisch steht in der Mitte.
items.sentence_translation: The table stands in the middle.
items.grammar_tip: 'In der Mitte' is a fixed phrase meaning 'in the center'.

items.sentence_de: Wir brauchen neue Möbel für das Wohnzimmer.
items.sentence_translation: We need new furniture for the living room.
items.grammar_tip: 'Möbel' is usually used in the plural.

items.sentence_de: Ich möchte bitte eine Pizza bestellen.
items.sentence_translation: I would like to order a pizza, please.
items.grammar_tip: 'Möchten' is technically the subjunctive of 'mögen' but used as 'would like'.

items.sentence_de: Einen Moment bitte, ich komme gleich.
items.sentence_translation: One moment please, I'm coming right away.
items.grammar_tip: 'Im Moment' means 'at the moment' or 'currently'.

items.sentence_de: Morgen habe ich leider keine Zeit.
items.sentence_translation: Tomorrow I unfortunately have no time.
items.grammar_tip: Do not confuse 'morgen' (tomorrow) with 'der Morgen' (the morning).

items.sentence_de: Jeden Morgen trinke ich einen Tee.
items.sentence_translation: Every morning I drink a tea.
items.grammar_tip: Times of day are masculine (except 'die Nacht').

items.sentence_de: Ich bin müde und gehe jetzt schlafen.
items.sentence_translation: I am tired and am going to sleep now.
items.grammar_tip: Used with the verb 'sein' (to be).

items.sentence_de: Bitte machen Sie den Mund weit auf.
items.sentence_translation: Please open your mouth wide.
items.grammar_tip: 'Mund' is masculine. The plural is 'Münder'.

items.sentence_de: Meine Mutter wohnt in einer kleinen Stadt.
items.sentence_translation: My mother lives in a small town.
items.grammar_tip: The plural 'Mütter' takes an umlaut.

items.sentence_de: Ich frage nach dem Weg zum Bahnhof.
items.sentence_translation: I am asking for the way to the station.
items.grammar_tip: 'Nach' is a dative preposition.

items.sentence_de: Mein Name ist Thomas Müller.
items.sentence_translation: My name is Thomas Müller.
items.grammar_tip: This is a masculine n-declension noun.

items.sentence_de: Ich nehme das Brötchen und ein Ei.
items.sentence_translation: I'll take the roll and an egg.
items.grammar_tip: 'Nehmen' is irregular: ich nehme, du nimmst, er nimmt.

items.sentence_de: Nein, das ist nicht meine Tasche.
items.sentence_translation: No, that is not my bag.
items.grammar_tip: Used to answer a yes/no question negatively.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe ein neues Handy gekauft.
items.sentence_translation: I bought a new mobile phone.
items.grammar_tip: The opposite of 'neu' is 'alt'.

items.sentence_de: Ich habe heute noch nichts gegessen.
items.sentence_translation: I have eaten nothing yet today.
items.grammar_tip: 'Nichts' is an indeclinable pronoun.

items.sentence_de: Er trinkt nie Kaffee am Abend.
items.sentence_translation: He never drinks coffee in the evening.
items.grammar_tip: 'Nie' is the strongest negation of frequency.

items.sentence_de: Kennst du noch andere Berufe?
items.sentence_translation: Do you know any other occupations?
items.grammar_tip: Used here to mean 'additional' or 'else'.

items.sentence_de: Das ist ein ganz normaler Tag.
items.sentence_translation: That is a completely normal day.
items.grammar_tip: 'Normal' is used similarly to English.

items.sentence_de: Wie ist deine Nummer vom Handy?
items.sentence_translation: What is your mobile number?
items.grammar_tip: 'Nummer' (die) is used for ID, telephone, or house numbers.

items.sentence_de: Das Ticket kostet nur fünf Euro.
items.sentence_translation: The ticket only costs five euros.
items.grammar_tip: Used to limit a quantity or express 'just'.

items.sentence_de: Die Toilette ist im ersten Stock oben.
items.sentence_translation: The toilet is upstairs on the first floor.
items.grammar_tip: Opposite of 'unten'. Describes location.

items.sentence_de: Zum Frühstück esse ich meistens Obst.
items.sentence_translation: For breakfast, I mostly eat fruit.
items.grammar_tip: 'Obst' is a collective noun and usually singular.

items.sentence_de: Das Wetter ist heute toll, oder?
items.sentence_translation: The weather is great today, right?
items.grammar_tip: Used at the end of a sentence like a tag question.

items.sentence_de: Können Sie bitte das Fenster öffnen?
items.sentence_translation: Can you please open the window?
items.grammar_tip: 'Öffnen' is the opposite of 'schließen'.

items.sentence_de: Gehst du oft ins Kino?
items.sentence_translation: Do you go to the cinema often?
items.grammar_tip: Indicates high frequency.

items.sentence_de: Ich trinke meinen Tee ohne Zucker.
items.sentence_translation: I drink my tea without sugar.
items.grammar_tip: 'Ohne' always takes the accusative case.

items.sentence_de: Meine Oma backt den besten Kuchen.
items.sentence_translation: My grandma bakes the best cake.
items.grammar_tip: Informal word for 'Großmutter'.

items.sentence_de: Mein Opa erzählt immer lustige Geschichten.
items.sentence_translation: My grandpa always tells funny stories.
items.grammar_tip: Informal word for 'Großvater'.

items.sentence_de: In welchem Ort wohnst du?
items.sentence_translation: In which place/village do you live?
items.grammar_tip: 'Ort' can mean a specific spot or a small town/village.

items.sentence_de: Haben Sie ein Blatt Papier für mich?
items.sentence_translation: Do you have a sheet of paper for me?
items.grammar_tip: 'Das Papier' is neuter.

items.sentence_de: Bringen Sie bitte alle wichtigen Papiere mit.
items.sentence_translation: Please bring all important documents with you.
items.grammar_tip: In the plural, 'Papiere' often refers to IDs or official documents.

items.sentence_de: Am Samstag machen wir eine große Party.
items.sentence_translation: On Saturday we are having a big party.
items.grammar_tip: Loanword from English; feminine gender in German.

items.sentence_de: Wir machen jetzt 15 Minuten Pause.
items.sentence_translation: We are taking a 15-minute break now.
items.grammar_tip: Commonly used for lunch or coffee breaks.

items.sentence_de: Die Kinder essen am liebsten Pommes frites.
items.sentence_translation: The children like eating fries the most.
items.grammar_tip: Usually just called 'Pommes'. Plural only.

items.sentence_de: Wo ist die Post? Ich muss ein Paket schicken.
items.sentence_translation: Where is the post office? I have to send a parcel.
items.grammar_tip: 'Die Post' refers to the mail system or the building.

items.sentence_de: Wie ist die Postleitzahl von Berlin?
items.sentence_translation: What is the zip code for Berlin?
items.grammar_tip: Often abbreviated as PLZ in Germany.

items.sentence_de: Der Preis für den Kaffee ist hoch.
items.sentence_translation: The price for the coffee is high.
items.grammar_tip: 'Der Preis' is masculine; plural remains 'die Preise'.

items.sentence_de: Kein Problem, ich helfe dir gerne.
items.sentence_translation: No problem, I am happy to help you.
items.grammar_tip: 'Das Problem' is neuter; its plural is 'Probleme'.

items.sentence_de: Morgen habe ich eine wichtige Prüfung.
items.sentence_translation: Tomorrow I have an important exam.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine.

items.sentence_de: Der Zug kommt heute sehr pünktlich.
items.sentence_translation: The train is coming very punctually today.
items.grammar_tip: Adjectives stay the same when used as adverbs.

items.sentence_de: Hier im Haus darf man nicht rauchen.
items.sentence_translation: One is not allowed to smoke here in the house.
items.grammar_tip: Verbs in the infinitive form always end in -en or -n.

items.sentence_de: Zahlen Sie die Rechnung bitte bar?
items.sentence_translation: Will you pay the bill in cash, please?
items.grammar_tip: Feminine noun ending in -ung; plural takes -en.

items.sentence_de: Die Post ist auf der Seite rechts.
items.sentence_translation: The post office is on the right side.
items.grammar_tip: Directional adverbs like 'rechts' are not capitalized.

items.sentence_de: Ich mag den Regen im Herbst.
items.sentence_translation: I like the rain in autumn.
items.grammar_tip: Weather phenomena are usually masculine.

items.sentence_de: Es wird heute den ganzen Tag regnen.
items.sentence_translation: It will rain all day today.
items.grammar_tip: The impersonal 'es' is used for weather verbs.

items.sentence_de: Ich esse gerne Fleisch mit viel Reis.
items.sentence_translation: I like eating meat with lots of rice.
items.grammar_tip: 'Der Reis' is a mass noun and rarely used in plural.

items.sentence_de: Gute Reise und viel Spaß in Berlin!
items.sentence_translation: Have a good trip and have fun in Berlin!
items.grammar_tip: 'Die Reise' is feminine; plural is 'Reisen'.

items.sentence_de: Der Reiseführer zeigt uns die alte Stadt.
items.sentence_translation: The travel guide shows us the old city.
items.grammar_tip: Masculine agent nouns ending in -er stay the same in plural.

items.sentence_de: Wir reisen im Sommer oft nach Spanien.
items.sentence_translation: We often travel to Spain in the summer.
items.grammar_tip: Regular verb: ich reise, du reist, er/sie/es reist.

items.sentence_de: Das Restaurant hat heute leider geschlossen.
items.sentence_translation: The restaurant is unfortunately closed today.
items.grammar_tip: Nouns of foreign origin are often neuter ('das').

items.sentence_de: Fragen Sie bitte an der Rezeption nach.
